html:
Agile ceremonies are where the BA's backlog work in Phase 6 gets consumed — plan the sprint, coordinate the day, inspect the outcome, and improve the process. This phase teaches you what each ceremony is for, how to prepare and run it, and where the business analyst adds value in each. BrightLogistics runs Scrum-style sprints of two weeks, so every example below is set in their lead-rollout project, and every tip you learn feeds directly into the daylight of a sprint review demo.

Learning Objectives

  • Describe the Scrum roles, events, and artifacts as a connected system...
  • Prepare a backlog that makes sprint planning a commitment, not a gamble...
  • Facilitate a daily standup that coordinates work in under 15 minutes...
  • Build a sprint review that demos against acceptance criteria and gets the business to say "done"...
  • Drive a retrospective that produces owned, actionable improvements...
  • Handle mid-sprint priority changes without encouraging chaos...
  • Use the repo's story-status flow, Stakeholder RACI model, and Task records as ceremony artifacts...
  • Apply facilitation techniques — agendas, parking lots, and decisions with owners — in every ceremony...

1. The Scrum Framework: Roles, Events, Artifacts

Scrum is a framework for organizing iterative delivery around a small, cross-functional team. It names three roles, four to five events, and three artifacts. For the BA the important insight is that they are a system: the backlog feeds planning, planning feeds the sprint, the standup coordinates the sprint, the review inspects the sprint, the retrospective improves the process, and the backlog receives the results.

EventPurposeBA focus
Sprint planningCommit to scope for the sprintRefined stories, clear acceptance criteria
Daily standupCoordinate, 15 minutesUnblock questions, clarify intent
Sprint reviewInspect the outcome with stakeholdersDemo against acceptance criteria
RetrospectiveImprove the processListen, capture actions with owners
Backlog refinementPrepare the next sprintReprioritize, slice, clarify stories

A sprint is a time box, typically 1-4 weeks; BrightLogistics uses two. Work that does not fit does not enter the sprint — that discipline is what makes the sprint data meaningful, because the review can honestly compare plan to outcome.

2. The Scrum Team Roles

The Product Owner owns value: they set priorities, represent the business, and decide what ships. The Scrum Master / facilitator owns the process: they remove obstacles and keep the ceremonies effective. The Developers (in Scrum language, anyone who builds — including BAs, designers, admins, and QA) own how: they estimate, implement, and validate.

The business analyst sits at the seam. The BA is the team's memory of WHY. In every ceremony, anchor the discussion to the user's need, not the solution — when a developer proposes "we add a field instead", the BA recalls the "so that" clause and asks whether the field actually serves it. The BA is usually the one who wrote, refined, scored, and demoed the stories, so the team treats the BA as the living traceability between business context and delivered behavior.

Where the BA is also the PM for the business relationship (as in many BrightLogistics projects), the same person may hold both the Product Owner-style backlog and the BA analysis duties. When roles blur, keep the ceremony distinct: planning decisions stay value-first, and the whole team sees the BL/criteria status clear.

3. Backlog Refinement

Refinement is the ceremony where stories get ready for a future sprint. It is the highest-leverage place a BA spends time because it prevents most other ceremony failures: a chronic 40-minute standup usually means stories entering the sprint were not refined, so the daily becomes a requirements meeting.

In refinement the team answers three questions for the incoming batch of stories:

  • Is it understood? The team can describe the workflow, the data, and the edge cases.
  • Is it small? Two days or less; otherwise re-slice on the spot.
  • Is it ranked? Priority_Score__c is current and the story map has no critical gaps.

Outputs are concrete: resized stories, sharpened acceptance criteria, recomputed scores, and a crisp "ready" list. Use the Backlog_Prioritization_Scoring flow from Phase 6 to re-rank and the User_Story_Status_Transition flow to move stories from Backlog to Refined. Refine the next 5-10 stories, not the whole backlog, and give every change an owner before the session ends.

4. Sprint Planning

Sprint planning decides what fits in the next sprint. It works only if the backlog arrived refined: the team takes stories from the top of the ready list and sizes them against the team's known velocity — the amount of work the team has empirically completed per sprint.

The planning agenda runs in two halves. First, the what: the team reviews the goal, the top stories, and their acceptance criteria, and selects the set that fulfills the value goal. Second, the how: the team breaks stories into tasks, assigns owners, and confirms the sprint backlog of committed work.

The BA's job in planning:

  • Present the stories with their criteria and scores — the facts, not salesmanship.
  • Enforce "ready": a story without verifiable criteria does not enter the sprint.
  • Record decisions and owners (RACI instinct from the Stakeholder__c model) so nothing escapes as rumor.

A common warning: a single invisible epic sliding in as "the last thing we add" drags the sprint down. If a story was not refined, it is not eligible.

5. Daily Standup

The daily standup is a coordination pulse, not a status report to the manager and not a problem-solving session. Each person answers three questions in about a minute: What did I do yesterday? What will I do today? What is blocking me?

The BA's role is light but specific: when a blocker is actually a requirements ambiguity ("does the dispatcher see this field on mobile too?"), the BA takes it to refinement instead of solving it in the standup. If the team's standup routinely runs 40 minutes, the BA treats that as a signal — stories are not refined — and fixes the backlog, not the standup.

Keep the ceremony short and standing. A visible board (physical or the Salesforce list view) beats a chat scroll. One conversation at a time; use the parking lot (section 9) for anything that needs more than two minutes.

6. Sprint Review

The sprint review is the inspection ceremony with the business. The team demonstrates what it shipped and the business decides whether the sprint goal was met. The demo anchors on the acceptance criteria accepted by the business:

"Here is the story. Here is the criterion. Does it pass?"

A review that demos against shared, written criteria keeps the verdict objective. The business owner says "done", not the developer — the BA keeps the acceptance-criteria checklist visible on the screen or on the board and drives the demo story by story. If a criterion fails in the review, that is data: either the story is not done (return to backlog) or the criterion was written wrong (renegotiate now, not next sprint).

The review also collects feedback for the backlog. New ideas that arise here go to refinement, not into the current sprint. BrightLogistics' go-live reviews this is how adoption feedback became the follow-up story backlog.

7. Retrospective

The retrospective answers "how do we work better next sprint?" — it looks at the process, not the product. The most reliable lightweight format is Start / Stop / Continue: the team votes on actions under each heading, and every action gets an owner and a landing ceremony.

md
Retro board (sample)
[Stop]   - No new stories sneaked in mid-sprint     -> PM
[Start]  - Demo every story against criteria        -> BA
[Continue] - Daily standup max 15 min               -> Team

A retrospective that produces no actions is decoration — but so is an action list nobody reads next sprint. The BA's moves in the retro:

  • Listen without defending; treat every finding as information.
  • Capture decisions and owners visibly (RACI instinct again).
  • Ensure each action has a "land" in a future ceremony — a Stop action should appear in the next planning as a rule.

Where the repo helps: the Task standard object (force-app/main/default/objects/Task/) is the natural home for retro actions with due dates and owners, and the User_Story_Status_Transition flow keeps story statuses truthful so the team can inspect real outcomes, not imagined ones.

8. The BA's Role in Each Ceremony

CeremonyPrepareRunFollow up
RefinementRe-score, re-slice, flag INVEST breaksClarify criteria, record ownersUpdate User_Story__c statuses
PlanningPresent ready stories + scoresEnforce "ready", capture commitmentsPublish sprint backlog
StandupKnow today's blockersRoute questions, apply parking lotFeed items to refinement
ReviewPrepare demo script vs criteriaDemo story/criterion verdictsLog feedback to backlog
RetroCollect the sprint dataFacilitate Start/Stop/ContinueLand actions as Tasks

The BA is the connective tissue: stories to criteria, criteria to demos, demos to feedback, feedback to backlog. Where a ceremony fails, inspect the artifact that fed it — most ceremony failures are backlog failures.

9. Facilitation: Facilitate, Don't Lecture

A ceremony leader sets the stage and draws out the crowd; they do not perform the meeting. Five habits make every ceremony better:

  1. Set a clear outcome for the meeting in the invite — "decide sprint scope" not "planning".
  2. Keep a visible agenda and a parking lot for tangents — note it, park it, return to it after the ceremony or in a dedicated conversation.
  3. Run one conversation at a time and call on the quiet ones; the person who says least often knows most.
  4. Close with explicit decisions and owners — every decision has a name attached.
  5. Time-box everything. A planning that overruns is a refining miss; a standup that overruns is a coordination failure.

The parking lot is the single highest-value tool: a tangent that keeps replaying in planning belongs on the parking lot and in a dedicated follow-up, not in the ceremony's dead air. When the same tangent returns at the next ceremony, the BA's unparked item from last time is the proof the follow-up never happened — make it an agenda item explicitly.

10. Handling Changing Priorities Without Chaos

Businesses change; BrightLogistics' founder Greg reprioritizes when a large freight client lands. The discipline that keeps priority changes orderly:

  • Strategy: keep the sprint sacred. A story already in the sprint changes only when the change is a genuine emergency; otherwise it waits for the next sprint planning and the Product Owner negotiates an explicit swap (one story out, one in).
  • Tactics: re-score immediately. When the business context changes, re-run the Backlog_Prioritization_Scoring flow on the affected stories, so the backlog reflects the new reality before the next planning.
  • Communication: name the trade. Every reprioritization costs something; state the deferred story out loud so the whole team — and the stakeholder — owns the cost, captured as a Task or backlog note.

The goal is not to freeze priorities but to make the process for changing them visible and cheap. When the team trusts that a real emergency can change the plan without a political fight, fake emergencies stop being tried.

11. Ceremony Artifacts in the Repository

The lab org models the ceremony life cycle so you can practise it declaratively:

  • User_Story_Status_Transition flow — force-app/main/default/flows/User_Story_Status_Transition.flow-meta.xml — moves stories Backlog -> Refined -> In Progress -> Done and enforces the gates (a story must be refined before In Progress).
  • Stakeholder__c with RACI__c, Influence__c, Interest__c — force-app/main/default/objects/Stakeholder__c/ — the role/accountability model you reuse to assign owners in planning, reviews, and retros.
  • Task — force-app/main/default/objects/Task/ — standard records carrying retro actions and demo decisions with due dates and owners.
  • UAT_Test_Case__c and the UAT_Defect_Logging flow — the review's "does it pass?" becomes a test case record and a defect log, which is where sprint review connects to Phase 12.

Together they are a working trace: story status, owner accountability, actions, and acceptance verdicts all live as data the next ceremony can inspect.

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 7.1 — Run a Sprint Planning with a Refined Backlog

Steps:

  1. Reset the four User_Story__c records from Phase 6 to Backlog status via the User_Story_Status_Transition flow.
  2. With a study group, run planning for a two-week sprint: select the ready stories, size them, and assign owners.
  3. Record the committed sprint scope and the deferred stories, each with a reason.

Expected result: a sprint commitment with explicit owners and an explicit "not this sprint" list. What it proves: refined stories make planning a decision, not a negotiation. (Sprint-planning variants appear in exercises 7.1 of Phase 15.)

Exercise 7.2 — Demo Against Acceptance Criteria

Steps:

  1. Take one story with Given/When/Then criteria from Phase 6's exercise 6.2.
  2. Prepare a three-screen demo script that walks the story and reads each criterion aloud.
  3. Run the review, and have a peer raise a mid-demo change request to practice the parking-lot response.

Expected result: the demo finishes with a written verdict per criterion and a parked change request. What it proves: review verdicts belong to the business owner and the criteria.

Exercise 7.3 — Retro That Produces Owned Actions

Steps:

  1. After exercise 7.1, run a 15-minute Start/Stop/Continue retro for the planning you just did.
  2. Vote on the actions, assign an owner to every one, and create a Task record for each action with a due date.
  3. Check that every Stop action is built into next planning's rules.

Expected result: a visible action board with owners, all landing in a future ceremony. What it proves: a retro without surfaced, owned, landing actions is decoration. (Deepen this with the ceremony combos in 7.3 of Phase 15.)

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
SprintA time-boxed iteration, typically 1-4 weeks, that produces a releasable increment.
CeremonyA Scrum event: planning, standup, review, retro, refinement.
Product backlogThe ordered list of stories awaiting scheduling.
Sprint backlogThe stories committed for the current sprint plus their tasks.
VelocityThe team's empirical throughput that planning uses to select scope.
Definition of DoneThe shared bar a story must clear before it counts as done.
Parking lotA visible list that holds tangents until after the ceremony.
Sprint reviewThe business-facing demo against acceptance criteria.
RetrospectiveThe team-facing process-improvement ceremony producing owned actions.
RACIResponsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed — the accountability model for decisions

Certification Checkpoints

  • Explain the purpose and BA focus of each of the five ceremonies...
  • Prepare a sprint planning by refining, sizing, and scoring the backlog in advance...
  • Facilitate a standup that coordinates in 15 minutes and parks requirements questions...
  • Run a sprint review where the business owner confirms done against written criteria...
  • Drive a Start/Stop/Continue retro where every action has an owner and a landing ceremony...
  • Manage a mid-sprint priority change with a named trade and a re-scored backlog...
  • Map the repo's story-status flow, RACI model, and Task records onto the ceremonies...

Summary

You now understand Agile ceremonies as one system fed by a healthy backlog: refinement prepares, planning commits, the standup coordinates, the review produces the business's verdict, and the retrospective improves the process — with the BA carrying the WHY through all of it. You can use the User_Story_Status_Transition flow, the Stakeholder__c RACI model, and Task records to make every ceremony's outcome verifiable data. That is Collaboration & Communication in practice, and it prepares every one of your demos for the reporting that Phase 10 will turn into evidence.
